Expected-output / assertion pass rates (high confidence throughout):
- bedrock-sec-kb-vector-not-failed: both 100% on expected output, but assertions 12/12 (with_skill) vs 6/12 (without_skill) — without_skill failed the "cites check ID" and "gives N/A" regex checks every time, while both passed the two LLM-judged behavioral assertions consistently (those two assertions discriminate nothing between variants).

One assertion ("does not cite retired check BR-09") passed for both every time, so it isn't discriminating.
- bedrock-sec-custom-model-single-finding: with_skill 100%/12-12; without_skill 0% expected-output, 3/8 assertions (note denominator differs — only 2/3 without_skill runs produced scorable output). One assertion was flaky for without_skill (1/2 pass, medium confidence) and one assertion passed for both.
- bedrock-sec-grounding-needs-rag: with_skill 100%/9-9; without_skill 33% expected-output, 3/9 assertions, with two assertions flaky (partial passes) rather than uniformly failing.
- bedrock-sec-vpc-endpoint-gated: with_skill 100%/9-9; without_skill 0%/0-9 — complete failure on this eval for without_skill.
- bedrock-sec-iam-user-visibility: with_skill 100%/12-12; without_skill 100% expected-output but only 6/12 assertions — it failed the check-ID-citation and N/A-format regex checks, but passed the two substantive LLM-judged behavior assertions (both variants passed those), so the failures here are narrower/formatting-related rather than behavioral.
- bedrock-sec-stale-access-prescribe-only: with_skill 100%/12-12; without_skill complete failure, 0% expected-output and 0/12 assertions.
- bedrock-sec-iam-action-prefix: both variants tied at 100% expected-output and 6/9 (67%) assertions — identical pass rates, including one assertion ("does not name a bedrock-agent IAM action") that failed for both variants every time, indicating that assertion or underlying behavior needs attention regardless of variant. Trigger itself only fired 2/3 times for this eval.

Quality comparisons (LLM-judged, mostly medium confidence, limited pairs): where evaluated, with_skill was favored more often on accuracy and actionability; without_skill was favored more often on completeness in two evals (iam-user-visibility, iam-action-prefix), and favored overall on the latter. Many quality comparisons were skipped (3 pairs skipped each in several evals) because without_skill's expected-output failures made the comparison inapplicable, so quality comparison data is thin and shouldn't be read as broad confirmation either way.

Runtime and cost: differences are small and inconsistent in direction — with_skill was faster/cheaper in some evals (e.g., vpc-endpoint-gated: 6s/$0.05 vs 10s/$0.09; kb-vector-not-failed: 8s/$0.07 vs 11s/$0.10) and slower/costlier in others (e.g., iam-user-visibility: 8s/$0.07 vs 4s/$0.04; kb-managed-cmk: 11s/$0.09 vs 9s/$0.08). No runs exceeded the 30s threshold in any eval where runtime comparison was run.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was generally "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" for both variants wherever measured, with high confidence; without_skill was occasionally rated fully "consistent" (e.g., kb-managed-cmk, iam-user-visibility, stale-access-prescribe-only) even in evals where its assertion/expected-output pass rate was very low or zero — meaning without_skill was reliably and repeatably failing those assertions rather than failing intermittently. One eval (custom-model-single-finding) could not compute a consistency score for without_skill (null), and iam-action-prefix could not compute one for with_skill (null), so those are missing rather than negative data points.

Three evals (neg-sagemaker, neg-access-denied, neg-adoption) were should_trigger:false negative tests; expected-output, assertions, metrics, comparison, and consistency were all marked skipped by design, so they contribute no variant comparison data. Trigger-fired rates for these were 100%, 100%, and 33% respectively, but since the downstream dimensions are skipped, this is just informational, not a performance signal on either variant.

Overall shape of the evidence: on most scored evals, with_skill met expected output and assertions more often, often sharply (several 100% vs 0% assertion gaps), with high-confidence measurements. On one eval (iam-action-prefix) the two variants tied exactly on expected-output and assertion rates, with quality judging slightly favoring without_skill on completeness. Timing/cost differences are mixed and modest, not a consistent tradeoff in either direction. Where quality comparisons were computed, with_skill tended to lead on accuracy/actionability and without_skill on completeness, but sample sizes for these comparisons are small (1–3 pairs) and confidence is medium, so this part of the picture is weaker evidence than the assertion-level pass-rate findings.

bedrock-sec-kb-vector-not-failed.summary:
Both variants fired the trigger in all 3 runs, and both met the overall "expected output" criterion in all 3 runs with high-confidence judgments — so at the top-level outcome measure there is no difference.

Where the two variants diverge clearly is in the per-assertion pass rates: with_skill passed all 12 assertions (100%), while without_skill passed only 6 of 12 (50%). Breaking this down by assertion shows an important pattern a single aggregate would hide:
- Two assertions ("The response says the knowledge base must not be reported as unencrypted..." and "The response does not report Failed or High severity for this VECTOR knowledge base") passed 3/3 for both variants with high confidence — these assertions don't distinguish the variants at all; both handle this correctly.
- Two other assertions ("Cites check ID BR-18" and "Gives N/A") passed 3/3 for with_skill but 0/3 for without_skill. This is a consistent, clean split across all three repeated runs, not a one-off fluke, suggesting without_skill systematically omits or fails to produce this specific content (citing the check ID and giving an N/A response) even though it still satisfies the broader expected-output check.

On quality comparison (3 pairs evaluated, none skipped), with_skill was favored more often overall (5 favorable judgments vs. 2 for without_skill, with 2 rated comparable), at medium average confidence. Looking per-criterion: accuracy favored with_skill in all 3 pairs; actionability and completeness were each split evenly (1 favoring with_skill, 1 favoring without_skill, 1 comparable) — so the quality edge for with_skill is concentrated in accuracy, while actionability and completeness show no consistent difference.

On efficiency, with_skill was faster (~8s vs ~11s average runtime) and cheaper (~$0.07 vs ~$0.10 average cost). Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in any of the 3 evaluated pairs. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.9% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs was identical for both variants: both rated "mostly_consistent" overall with the same score (2.67) and the same dimension breakdown (2 consistent, 1 mostly_consistent), at high confidence — so neither variant showed more run-to-run variability than the other.

Overall, this is a small eval (3 runs/pairs), so findings should be read with some caution regarding sample size, though confidence levels reported for individual measurements are mostly high (quality comparison is medium confidence). The main substantive difference is that without_skill consistently failed two specific, narrowly-scoped assertions (citing BR-18 and giving N/A) that with_skill consistently passed, while with_skill also ran faster, cost less, and was favored more often on quality (primarily driven by accuracy). Other dimensions — expected-output attainment, the two shared-passing assertions, runtime threshold compliance, and output consistency — showed no difference between the variants.

bedrock-sec-kb-managed-cmk.summary:
This evaluation covered a single chat task (3 repeated runs), checking whether the agent correctly identifies and reports on knowledge-base encryption findings in Bedrock (citing check BR-18, correctly flagging kb-a as Passed with its customer-managed key ARN, kb-b as Failed/High severity, and avoiding duplicate findings or a retired check ID).

The behavior under test fired reliably in all 3 runs (trigger_fired 3/3) for both variants, so there's a solid basis for comparison.

On expected output and assertions, there is a large and consistent gap: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence) and passed all 15 assertion checks (15/15, 100%). without_skill failed to meet the expected output in any run (0/3, high confidence) and passed only 3 of 15 assertion checks (20%). Breaking this down by individual assertion: one assertion ("does not cite the retired duplicate check BR-09") passed for both variants in all runs — this check isn't distinguishing the two. The other four assertions (citing BR-18, reporting kb-a as Passed with the correct key ARN, reporting kb-b as Failed/High, and avoiding a duplicate finding for kb-b) all passed consistently for with_skill and failed consistently for without_skill across all 3 runs. All of these judgments were made with high confidence, so the measurement itself appears reliable, not just a low-confidence artifact.

On runtime and cost, the two variants were close: with_skill averaged 11s and $0.09 per run, without_skill averaged 9s and $0.08 per run — a small difference (~2s, ~$0.01) in without_skill's favor. Context window utilization was low for both (6.2% vs 4.7%), with no compaction events for either.

Quality comparison data was not usable here: all 3 pairs were skipped and none were evaluated, so no quality-favoring signal is available in either direction.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability of each variant's own outputs, independent of correctness) was high for both: without_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0) across all three dimensions, while with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.67, two dimensions consistent, one mostly consistent) — both are high-confidence ratings and the difference is minor.

Overall, the main finding is a substantial difference in task correctness: with_skill satisfied the expected output and nearly all assertions, while without_skill did not meet the expected output in any run and failed most assertions tied to specific factual details (check ID citation, pass/fail status reporting, key ARN citation, duplicate finding suppression). This correctness gap is large and consistent across repeated runs, while cost, runtime, and output consistency differences between the two variants are comparatively minor and don't offset the correctness gap in either direction. No quality-comparison data was available to weigh further.
